The core concept revolves around distinguishing between apparent and true means in statistical sampling. In small Fraternities, the apparent mean (MF) fluctuates widely due to finite-size effects, whereas the true mean (MF_true) emerges only in the limit of infinite size. This duality implies that estimating MF_true requires extrapolation from increasingly larger samples. The process involves constructing an idealized, infinitely large Fraternity to define MF_true, then drawing finite samples to approximate it. Each sample yields an (MF'), and these values form a distribution centered on MF_true. The deviation of individual (MF') from MF_true follows a predictable pattern governed by the scaling factor b and square root of sample size n. Thus, the primitive 'Apparent Mean Convergence' captures how MF approaches MF_true, while 'Sample Variance Scaling' describes the probabilistic spread of estimates around the true mean. These primitives together enable GSI to perform Bayesian inference on true parameters and GSE to reason about state transitions in response to changing sample sizes.
